title: Kayaking in Snowdonia
strapline: Snowdonia is whitewater country — short, steep, rain-fed rivers in glacier-cut valleys, plus the biggest natural lake in Wales for flat-water days.
metaTitle: Kayaking in Snowdonia | Whitewater & Lakes | Adventure Wales
metaDescription: Honest guide to kayaking in Snowdonia: the whitewater rivers (Afon Conwy, Llugwy, Glaslyn), flat-water on Llyn Tegid and Llyn Padarn, and where to learn with Plas y Brenin or Bala Adventure & Watersports.
heroAlt: Whitewater kayaker dropping into a rapid on the Afon Llugwy in Snowdonia, with autumn forest on the riverbanks.
introduction:
Up front: kayaking in Snowdonia means whitewater first, flat-water second, sea kayaking not at all. The Eryri national park is landlocked on three sides; the sea kayaking that British paddlers associate with North Wales — South Stack, Holy Island, the Llŷn Peninsula — all sits outside the park boundary. What Snowdonia does have, in concentration, is the run-off from the wettest mountain range in England and Wales: short, steep, rain-fed rivers draining through hard volcanic bedrock into the Conwy and Mawddach catchments. The result is a whitewater scene that the British Canoeing community has been paddling for decades and that's still one of the best-rated technical river venues in the UK.

The core whitewater is three rivers, all reachable from a Betws-y-Coed base. The Afon Conwy between Betws-y-Coed and Llanrwst is the regional benchmark — a continuous grade 3 (with a grade 4 'Conwy Falls' rapid that most paddlers walk first) that runs reliably from October through April and after any decent rain in summer. The Afon Llugwy through the Fairy Glen gorge above Betws is the connoisseurs' choice — tight, technical grade 3-4 in a deep wooded canyon, beautiful and unforgiving. The Afon Glaslyn out of Beddgelert runs through the Aberglaslyn Pass on grade 3-4 ledges and slots, with a famously committing eddy line at the railway bridge. None of these are summer flat-water rivers; they need rain in the previous 48 hours and they spike fast. River-level gauges (UK Rivers Guidebook, Natural Resources Wales) are the deciding factor on every day out.

For flat-water and learning, the picture flips. Llyn Tegid (Bala) is the largest natural lake in Wales — four miles long, sheltered by mountains, ideal for touring kayaks, recreational paddles and SUP. Llyn Padarn at Llanberis sits at the foot of Snowdon and runs a similar scene on a smaller scale. Bala Adventure & Watersports is the dedicated centre on Llyn Tegid (kayak hire, sailing, lessons), and Snowdonia Watersports runs the same product on Llyn Padarn. For structured tuition — beginner foundation, white-water progression, sea-kayak conversion courses — Plas y Brenin, the National Outdoor Centre at Capel Curig, is the single most credentialled paddling venue in Wales and the entry point most British paddlers use.

One practical note before you book: Snowdonia is not a self-guided destination for first-time paddlers. The flat-water lakes are fine for hire-and-go; the rivers are not. If you don't already have grade 3 whitewater experience and a local guidebook, take a course or a guided day — the Afon Conwy and Afon Llugwy in particular have killed competent paddlers who underestimated the level.
difficultyRange: Beginner (Bala/Padarn flat-water) to Expert (Glaslyn / Llugwy gorges)
topTips: Whitewater and flat-water are two different trips here — decide which one you're actually doing before you plan anything else. The rivers (Conwy, Llugwy, Glaslyn) need grade 3+ experience and recent rain; the lakes (Bala, Padarn, Gwynant) are hire-and-go for anyone.

Sea kayaking is not a Snowdonia activity, whatever the marketing implies — the national park is landlocked. If you came for coastal paddling, redirect to Anglesey (South Stack, Holy Island) or the Llŷn Peninsula; Plas y Brenin runs conversion courses out to both.

Check the river gauge before you drive anywhere near the Conwy, Llugwy or Glaslyn. The UK Rivers Guidebook and the Natural Resources Wales level pages are the two sources every local paddler actually checks — a dry week can mean no water at all.

None of the three whitewater rivers carry a confirmed public right of navigation — access sits in the same legally unresolved space as most non-tidal rivers in Wales. In practice paddlers have used them for decades without incident, but it's worth knowing the access position isn't settled law, unlike, say, the Wye.

If you're learning from scratch, start at Plas y Brenin, not on the rivers. The Conwy and Llugwy are step-up venues for people who already have grade 3 skills — they are not beginner water, and the Llugwy gorge in particular has claimed experienced paddlers who misjudged it.

Scout before you commit on all three rivers — Conwy Falls, the Llugwy's technical drops and the Aberglaslyn railway-bridge eddy line all have blind entries from the boat. Every spot's insider tip in this guide says the same thing for a reason.

On the lakes, launch early. Bala's open water turns choppy under the afternoon south-westerly, and Padarn and Gwynant get busier as the day goes on — morning sessions are calmer water and quieter car parks.

Cold water catches people out even in summer. Padarn and the rivers sit at 8-14°C year-round — wear a wetsuit or drysuit even on a warm day, and treat any capsize on the lakes as a genuine cold-shock risk, not just a soaking.

firstTimer: Work out which Snowdonia you're paddling before you book anything — whitewater river or flat-water lake. They need completely different kit, skills and weather, and this guide covers both.

If you have no whitewater experience, book a course at Plas y Brenin rather than attempting the rivers self-guided. It's the National Outdoor Centre and the standard UK entry point for a reason — the Conwy and Llugwy are not learner water.

For a first flat-water session, Llyn Tegid (Bala) or Llyn Padarn are the easiest options — both have walk-up hire, buoyancy aids included, and staff on hand. Bala Adventure & Watersports covers Tegid; Snowdonia Watersports covers Padarn.

Pack for cold water regardless of the season. River and lake temperatures sit at 8-14°C most of the year in Snowdonia — a wetsuit isn't optional kit here, it's the difference between a good day and a genuinely dangerous one.
Don't plan a whitewater day around a fixed date. These are rain-fed rivers with no dam release — check the gauges 24-48 hours out and be ready to swap to a lake day if the level's wrong.
Betws-y-Coed is the natural base for river days (train station, gear shops, cafes); Llanberis or Bala for lake days. Trying to cover both from one base means a lot of driving.
A buoyancy aid (PFD) is mandatory at every hire centre and every course — don't expect to skip it, and don't skip it if you bring your own boat either.

If you're driving from England, build in the shuttle-vehicle problem for river days — whitewater runs are point-to-point, so a self-guided trip needs two cars or a guided operator who handles the shuttle for you.
regular: The Llugwy's Fairy Glen-style gorge drops change character completely with water level — a clean line at medium-low becomes a sticky hole at high water. Re-scout on every visit, even ones you know well.
Weekday mornings are the move on both Bala and Padarn — car parks fill and wind picks up through the afternoon, especially on Bala's exposed open water.
Llyn Gwynant is the quiet alternative to Padarn if you're bringing your own boat — no commercial day-hire operator works the lake, so it stays markedly less busy even in peak season.
After a dry spell, don't write off a river day — 24-48 hours of decent rain on the catchment is often enough to bring the Conwy or Glaslyn up to a paddleable level even in summer.

The Aberglaslyn eddy line under the Welsh Highland Railway bridge is the read of the day on the Glaslyn — get it wrong and you're committed to the harder lower section with no inspection chance. Walk it from the riverside path first, every time.
For a lower-commitment intro to Snowdonia whitewater, the Fairy Glen-to-Llanrwst stretch on the lower Conwy scales down the classic run without the grade 4 falls section.
Combine a lake session with a river scout — paddle Padarn or Gwynant in the morning, then walk the Llugwy or Glaslyn banks in the afternoon to read the lines for your next trip up in grade.
The eastern (Llangower) shoreline on Bala is the sheltered side when the forecast is gusty — worth knowing if you've already driven out and the wind's picked up.

spots.name: Afon Conwy — Betws-y-Coed to Llanrwst
spots.description: The classic Snowdonia whitewater run — continuous grade 3 with a single significant grade 4 drop (the Conwy Falls section) that most parties walk. Nine kilometres of road-accessible river through a wooded valley, with a reliable rain window from October through April. Eddy-hop and play-boat sections, plus enough wave trains to give it big-river character. The standard 'introduction to North Wales whitewater' run for paddlers stepping up from southern English rivers.
spots.bestFor: Grade 3 paddlers wanting a continuous whitewater day; clubs and progression courses
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, paddlers without solid grade 3 eddy-hopping and rolling
spots.bestSeason: October-April, plus 24-48 hours after any heavy summer rain
spots.parking: Get-in: A5 layby above Conwy Falls (paid). Get-out: Llanrwst (free roadside near the bridge). Shuttle by car needed unless going with a guided operator.

startPoint.name: Conwy Falls get-in (above the falls portage)

spots.insiderTip: Walk Conwy Falls before you commit — sightlines on the entry boof are misleading from the boat. The lower section from Fairy Glen to Llanrwst makes a cleaner intro run if you want to scale down.
spots.howToDoIt: Get in above Conwy Falls, walk and inspect the falls drop before running or portaging it, then settle into a continuous grade 3 rhythm of eddy-hopping and wave trains down through the gorge to Llanrwst. Most parties run it as a single push rather than stopping to play, since the shuttle logistics reward getting off the water promptly. Solid grade 3 skills (confident eddy turns, a reliable roll) are the minimum; this is a step-up run for paddlers moving on from grade 2 rivers, not a first whitewater trip.
spots.routeDescription: From the get-in above the falls, the river drops through a wooded gorge with a near-continuous sequence of grade 3 rapids, broken by pools and eddies that let you regroup. The Conwy Falls drop itself is the one significant grade 4 feature — most parties walk it via the path rather than run it blind. Below the falls the gradient eases into the classic Fairy Glen-style gorge scenery, with the river opening out gradually as you approach Llanrwst and the take-out near the bridge.
spots.access: No confirmed public right of navigation exists on the Afon Conwy — like most non-tidal rivers in Wales, the legal access position is unresolved rather than guaranteed, though paddlers have used this stretch for decades without dispute. Get-in is via the A5 layby above Conwy Falls (small, paid, fits only a handful of cars); a mud layby on the river-left road below the Machno bridge gives a lower put-in above the first rapid if you want to skip the falls entirely. Get-out is free roadside parking near the Llanrwst bridge. A car shuttle is essential unless you're going with a guided operator.

spots.name: Afon Llugwy — Pont Cyfyng to Betws-y-Coed (Fairy Glen)
spots.description: The Llugwy is the technical end of Snowdonia whitewater — tight ledges and slots through the Fairy Glen gorge, grading at a hard 3 to soft 4 depending on level. Significantly more committing than the Conwy because the gorge walls cut off river-right escape options on several drops. Beautiful, tree-lined, and consistently rated one of the best technical short runs in Britain. Generally paddled by experienced grade 4 whitewater kayakers; not a 'step up from the Conwy' day.
spots.bestFor: Experienced grade 3-4 whitewater kayakers; coached progression days run by Plas y Brenin or independent guides
spots.notSuitableFor: Anyone without strong grade 4 paddling, a bombproof roll, and a competent team
spots.bestSeason: October-March in normal water; rain-dependent rest of year
spots.parking: Get-in: Pont Cyfyng layby (limited; arrive early). Get-out: Betws-y-Coed below the Pont-y-Pair bridge.
spots.insiderTip: The crux drops in the Glen change character with water level — what's a clean line at medium-low becomes a sticky hole at high. Scout from the riverside path before you get in.
spots.howToDoIt: This is a scout-first river, not a read-and-run one. Walk the gorge from the riverside path before getting on the water so the team knows the crux ledges and slots at the level on the day, then paddle it tight and committed — gorge walls remove most river-right escape options once you're in. Run it with a competent group who can set up rescue positions above the harder drops; this is coached-progression or experienced-team territory, not a solo or casual outing.
spots.routeDescription: From the Pont Cyfyng get-in, the river narrows into a wooded gorge of closely-spaced ledges and slots, graded a hard 3 to soft 4 depending on level. The crux sequence sits mid-gorge where the channel tightens and the drops come with little recovery water between them. Below the technical section the gradient eases toward Betws-y-Coed, finishing under the Pont-y-Pair bridge.
spots.access: As with the Conwy, there's no confirmed public right of navigation on this stretch of the Llugwy — access has long been used by paddlers without formal dispute, but it isn't a legally guaranteed right. Get-in at the Pont Cyfyng layby is limited to a few cars and fills early on weekends; arrive with time to spare or you'll be parking further out and walking boats in. Get-out is at Betws-y-Coed below the Pont-y-Pair bridge, a short walk from the village.

spots.name: Afon Glaslyn — Beddgelert through the Aberglaslyn Pass
spots.description: The Glaslyn through the Aberglaslyn Pass is one of the most scenic whitewater runs in Wales — the river squeezes through a tight wooded gorge below the Welsh Highland Railway, with grade 3-4 ledges, a famously committing eddy line at the railway bridge, and a portage option around the harder lower drops. Shorter than the Conwy and more atmospheric than the Llugwy. Paddled less often (smaller window, harder shuttle), but a benchmark Welsh river when it's on.
spots.bestFor: Experienced grade 3-4 whitewater paddlers; small competent teams
spots.notSuitableFor: Grade 2 paddlers, unsupported solo runs, anyone without recent rain to bring the level up
spots.bestSeason: October-March; needs significant rain in catchment
spots.parking: Get-in: Beddgelert village (multiple pay-and-display car parks). Get-out: Aberglaslyn Pass layby on A4085.
spots.estimatedCost: Free self-guided; guided trips run on demand from Plas y Brenin
spots.insiderTip: The railway-bridge eddy is the move of the day — get it wrong and you're swept into the harder lower section without an inspection chance. Walk the gorge from the riverside path before you launch.
spots.howToDoIt: Launch from Beddgelert and paddle down into the Aberglaslyn Pass, a tight wooded gorge that the Welsh Highland Railway also threads through on a ledge above the water. The defining move is the eddy line at the railway bridge — catching it correctly gives you the chance to inspect the harder lower ledges; missing it sweeps you straight into them uninspected. A clean portage option exists around the hardest lower drops for teams who want to keep the run within their comfort margin.
spots.routeDescription: From the Beddgelert bridge, the Glaslyn runs a short, sharp sequence of grade 3-4 ledges before the gorge properly closes in at the Aberglaslyn Pass. The railway bridge eddy marks the transition into the harder lower section; below it the river drops through further ledges and slots in the narrowest part of the gorge before opening out toward the A4085 take-out layby. Short at 4km, but concentrated — there's little flat water to recover in.
spots.access: The Glaslyn carries no confirmed public right of navigation either, the same unresolved position as most Welsh whitewater. The riverside path through the Aberglaslyn Pass is a popular walking route (National Trust-managed land), so expect walkers and photographers watching from the banks, especially near the railway bridge. Get-in is at Beddgelert village, which has multiple pay-and-display car parks; get-out is the layby on the A4085 at the pass. This river needs a genuinely wet catchment to run — it has the smallest and least predictable window of the three.

spots.name: Llyn Tegid (Bala Lake)
spots.description: The largest natural lake in Wales — four miles long, mountain-sheltered, and the obvious flat-water kayaking and SUP venue in the region. Hireable touring kayaks, sit-on-tops and SUPs from Bala Adventure & Watersports on the foreshore, plus structured lessons and guided sessions. Wind is the main variable — afternoon south-westerlies can push up significant chop on the open lake, so morning sessions are usually flatter. Wildlife includes the unique gwyniad whitefish (the lake is the only place in the world it lives).
spots.bestFor: Families, beginners, SUP, kayak touring, lessons
spots.notSuitableFor: Anyone wanting whitewater — this is sheltered flat-water
spots.bestSeason: April-October (lake is exposed in winter winds)
spots.estimatedCost: Kayak hire from approx £20-£30/hour; lessons from approx £40
spots.insiderTip: Launch from the foreshore early — by mid-afternoon the prevailing wind picks up and turns the open water choppy. The eastern (Llangower) shoreline is the sheltered side if the forecast looks gusty.
spots.howToDoIt: Walk up to Bala Adventure & Watersports on the foreshore, get fitted with a buoyancy aid and a touring kayak or SUP, and launch straight off the shore — no experience or booking-ahead required for casual hire, though lessons and guided sessions can be booked for more structure. First-timers should stay close to the foreshore; more confident paddlers can tour the full four-mile length or cross to the quieter Llangower shore.
spots.routeDescription: Llyn Tegid runs roughly four miles north-east to south-west, hemmed in by the Aran and Arenig ranges. The foreshore at the Bala end is the main launch and stays busiest; paddling south-west toward Llangower opens up quieter water and closer mountain views, with the sheltered eastern shore giving the best refuge if wind picks up on the open lake.
spots.access: Public lake with an established watersports centre — no access complications. Launch is directly off the Bala Lake foreshore car park (pay-and-display), a short walk from the town centre. No tides to consider; wind exposure on the open water is the only variable that changes access conditions day to day.

spots.name: Llyn Padarn
spots.description: Llanberis's two-mile lake at the foot of Snowdon — the flat-water kayaking and SUP venue most paddlers reach first because it sits next to Pete's Eats, the climbing scene, and the Llanberis Path trailhead. Snowdonia Watersports runs hire from a base on the lake shore (kayaks, SUPs, no motorboats). Water is glacial-clear and cold even in summer (8-12°C); the lake holds Arctic charr, a relic of the last ice age. The southern end runs into the National Slate Museum and the old Dinorwig Quarry workings — interesting paddle objective in itself.
spots.bestFor: Families based in Llanberis, lesson-shaped beginner sessions, post-Snowdon recovery paddles
spots.notSuitableFor: Anyone wanting whitewater or open-water touring distance
spots.bestSeason: April-October (cold even in summer — wear a wetsuit if you might capsize)
spots.parking: Pay-and-display car parks along the A4086 in Llanberis; the watersports centre has on-site parking for hire customers.
spots.insiderTip: Paddle the south-east shore for the best Dinorwig Quarry views — the abandoned slate workings tower above the water and make the most striking backdrop in the lake.
spots.howToDoIt: Hire is walk-up from the Snowdonia Watersports base on the lake shore — get kitted with a buoyancy aid and wetsuit (the water stays cold even in summer), then paddle out either direction. The lake is sheltered enough for a relaxed first-timer session, but the cold, deep water means a capsize is a genuine consideration, not just an inconvenience — wear the wetsuit even if you don't plan to go in.
spots.routeDescription: Llyn Padarn runs about two miles north-east to south-west below Snowdon. The south-eastern end, toward Llyn Peris and the old Dinorwig Quarry workings, has the most dramatic scenery — slate terraces rising straight from the water. The northern end runs out toward the National Slate Museum and the lake's outflow, a flatter, more open stretch.
spots.access: Public lake, no access complications. Launch from the Snowdonia Watersports base on the shore, with on-site parking for hire customers; additional pay-and-display parking runs along the A4086 through Llanberis. No tidal or navigation-rights issues — this is straightforward hire-and-go water.

spots.name: Plas y Brenin — Capel Curig coaching base
spots.description: Not a spot in the geographic sense — Plas y Brenin is the National Outdoor Centre at Capel Curig, and it's the central training venue for British paddlesport. The base runs from a private lake (Llynnau Mymbyr) directly outside the centre, with daily access to all three whitewater rivers above and the sea coast within an hour. Courses span beginner kayak / canoe foundation, whitewater progression (grade 2 through grade 4), white-water leader awards, BC coach progression, and sea-kayak transition courses. If you're learning paddlesport in the UK, this is the venue.
spots.bestFor: Anyone learning kayaking properly, qualification candidates, structured progression
spots.notSuitableFor: Drop-in casual hire — Plas y Brenin runs courses, not hourly rentals
spots.bestSeason: Year-round (winter whitewater progression is a flagship season here)
spots.parking: Plas y Brenin on-site car park.
spots.estimatedCost: Day courses from approx £100; residentials £400+ (includes meals and accommodation)
spots.insiderTip: Book the residential format if you can — the post-day debriefs in the bar (the Climber's Bar at PyB is a paddling institution in itself) are where most of the actual learning happens.
spots.howToDoIt: Book onto a graded course — beginner foundation if you've never paddled, whitewater progression if you've got flat-water skills and want to move onto rivers, or a sea-kayak conversion course if you're heading out to Anglesey or the Llŷn afterwards. Early sessions typically run on the on-site Llynnau Mymbyr lake to build core skills before the group moves onto graded whitewater on the Conwy, Llugwy or nearby rivers as conditions and ability allow.
spots.routeDescription: Not a single route — Plas y Brenin's paddling programme uses Llynnau Mymbyr immediately outside the centre for skills and rescue practice, then draws on the full spread of Snowdonia whitewater (Conwy, Llugwy, and other grade 2-4 rivers depending on level and water) for progression days, with the sea coast at Anglesey and the Llŷn available within about an hour for conversion courses.
spots.access: Plas y Brenin holds the access relationships and local knowledge to run river days appropriately for the group's ability and the day's water levels, which is one of the practical reasons to book a course here rather than working it out independently — especially given the unresolved public navigation rights on the surrounding rivers. On-site parking is provided for course attendees; the centre sits directly on the A5 at Capel Curig.

spots.name: Llyn Gwynant
spots.description: Quieter, wilder alternative to Padarn — a long sheltered lake in the Nant Gwynant valley below the Watkin Path, with a campsite at its head that hires SUPs and kayaks to guests. No commercial day-hire operator works the lake, so it stays markedly less busy than Padarn or Bala. Striking mountain backdrop (Yr Aran on one side, the Glyderau on the other) and clean, swimmable water. Good objective for a touring kayaker carrying their own boat.
spots.bestFor: Self-supported paddlers, campsite guests, anyone wanting a quieter lake than Padarn
spots.notSuitableFor: Day-trippers without their own boat — no on-site hourly hire
spots.parking: Llyn Gwynant campsite (paid day access) or the National Trust car park at the foot of the Watkin Path.
spots.estimatedCost: Free if bringing own boat; campsite SUP hire approx £15/hour
spots.insiderTip: Launch from the campsite end and paddle south-west — the head of the lake holds the best mountain views and the shallowest beach-style entries for swimming breaks.
spots.howToDoIt: If you're a campsite guest, hire a SUP or kayak on-site and launch straight off the shore. If you're bringing your own boat, pay for day access at the campsite or use the National Trust car park at the foot of the Watkin Path and carry down to the water. There's no lifeguard or hire desk beyond the campsite's own offering, so this suits confident, self-sufficient paddlers more than a first-timer session.
spots.routeDescription: A long, narrow lake in the Nant Gwynant valley, running roughly north-east to south-west beneath Yr Aran and the Glyderau. The head of the lake (campsite end) has the most sheltered water and shallow, beach-style entries; paddling the full length gives an increasingly open, mountain-framed run with the Watkin Path trailhead visible at the southern end.
spots.access: No commercial day-hire operator works this lake, so casual access depends on either being a campsite guest or bringing your own boat. Day access to launch from the campsite is a paid arrangement; the alternative is the National Trust car park at the foot of the Watkin Path, from where it's a short carry to the water. No tidal considerations — wind is the main variable, though the valley setting gives more shelter than Bala's open water.

practicalInfo.weather: Snowdonia weather drives kayaking decisions on every river. Whitewater needs rain in the previous 24-48 hours; flat-water lakes need calm wind. Spring snowmelt and autumn-winter rain are the most reliable seasons. Check river-level gauges and wind forecasts together — a sunny day with a 25mph south-westerly turns Bala Lake into chop.
gearChecklist: Whitewater kayak with airbags / sit-on-top / touring kayak — match the boat to the water
Spray deck (whitewater / closed cockpit boats only)
Buoyancy aid / PFD (mandatory on hire from all centres)
Helmet (whitewater rivers and gorges only — not needed on the flat-water lakes)
Wetsuit or drysuit — even summer river-water is 8-14°C in Snowdonia
Throw line (whitewater team kit — every party should have one)
Dry bag for car keys / phone / snacks
Spare clothes and a thermos of hot drink waiting in the get-out vehicle

driveTimes.route: M40 / M6 / A5 — most rivers reachable from a Betws-y-Coed base
M56 and A55, then A470 south into the park

gettingThere.publicTransport: Betws-y-Coed has a direct train station on the Conwy Valley Line (changes at Llandudno Junction from main coast services). Bala and Llanberis are not on the rail network — bus connections from Bangor or Wrexham. For whitewater shuttles you'll need at least one car in the party.
gettingThere.parkingTips: Whitewater get-ins on the A5 (Conwy Falls) and around Pont Cyfyng are small laybys — arrive early at weekends. The Bala foreshore and Llyn Padarn car parks are pay-and-display and fill on summer afternoons. Plas y Brenin has dedicated on-site parking for course attendees.

practicalInfo.safety: Snowdonia rivers are genuinely dangerous — they have killed competent paddlers in recent years. Never paddle whitewater here alone; check gauges, scout the harder drops, and walk anything you're not confident on. On the flat-water lakes, cold water is the real risk — a capsize in 8-12°C water without a wetsuit drops core temperature fast. Hire a buoyancy aid every time, even on a calm lake day. In emergencies dial 999 and ask for Mountain Rescue (river callouts are handled jointly with the local water-rescue team).

faqs.question: Is Snowdonia a good destination for sea kayaking?
faqs.answer: Not really — Snowdonia National Park is landlocked on three sides. The North Wales sea kayaking everyone associates with the region (South Stack, Holy Island, the Llŷn coast) is actually on Anglesey or the Llŷn Peninsula, both outside the park. If sea kayaking is your goal, base in Trearddur Bay (Anglesey) or Abersoch (Llŷn) instead of inside Eryri. Plas y Brenin runs sea-kayak conversion courses that travel out to those coasts.

faqs.question: When does the Afon Conwy have enough water to paddle?
faqs.answer: Reliably from October through April. In summer it needs 24-48 hours of significant rain on the catchment to bring it up. Check the UK Rivers Guidebook level page and the Natural Resources Wales Llanrwst gauge before you commit to a shuttle.

faqs.question: Can I learn to kayak in Snowdonia with no previous experience?
faqs.answer: Yes — Plas y Brenin at Capel Curig is the National Outdoor Centre and the standard UK venue for learn-to-kayak courses. Bala Adventure & Watersports and Snowdonia Watersports also run beginner sessions on the lakes. Don't try to learn on the rivers; the Snowdonia whitewater is a step-up venue, not a starter.

faqs.question: Is hire-and-go kayaking available?
faqs.answer: On the lakes, yes — Bala and Llyn Padarn both have walk-up kayak / SUP hire. On the rivers, no — there's no hire-and-go whitewater rental for the obvious safety reason. Whitewater access is via courses, guided trips, or BYO boat.

faqs.question: What grade of whitewater is the Afon Llugwy?
faqs.answer: Hard grade 3 to soft grade 4 through the Fairy Glen gorge section, depending on water level. The gorge cuts off many escape options, so it should only be paddled by experienced grade 3-4 paddlers with a strong roll and a competent team.

faqs.question: Is wild swimming OK on the kayaking rivers?
faqs.answer: Some pools yes (the Fairy Glen on the Llugwy is a popular swimming spot), but cross-reference with the [Snowdonia wild swimming combo](/snowdonia). When the rivers are at paddling level they're too pushy for safe swimming.

faqs.question: Do I need to be a British Canoeing member to paddle in Snowdonia?
faqs.answer: Membership isn't legally required for access (English / Welsh rivers don't have a paddle permit scheme like some European countries), but BC membership gives you third-party insurance and access to course discounts at Plas y Brenin. Most regular paddlers carry it.

gearShops.name: Joe Brown's
gearShops.description: Long-standing outdoor retailer at Capel Curig and Llanberis. Useful for paddling layers, drysuit hire enquiries, throw lines and accessories.

gearShops.name: V12 Outdoor
gearShops.description: Llanberis outdoor shop with technical clothing and accessories suitable for cold-water paddling.

gearShops.name: Summit to Sea
gearShops.description: Multi-discipline outdoor shop in Llanberis — paddling and watersports lines stocked alongside climbing and MTB.

postActivitySpots.name: Pete's Eats
postActivitySpots.description: The legendary climbers' and paddlers' cafe in Llanberis. Hot drinks, giant breakfasts and the unofficial debrief venue after any day on Llyn Padarn or the Llanberis rivers.

postActivitySpots.name: Caffi Siabod
postActivitySpots.description: On the A5 between Betws-y-Coed and Capel Curig, with views over Llynnau Mymbyr toward the Snowdon Horseshoe. Standard breakfast and brew stop before a Conwy or Llugwy run.

postActivitySpots.name: Plas y Brenin Climbers Bar
postActivitySpots.description: Bar and lounge inside the National Outdoor Centre. Where paddlers debrief at the end of a course day. Open to non-residents.

postActivitySpots.name: Y Stablau
postActivitySpots.description: Restaurant and bar in Betws-y-Coed, the natural meet-and-eat venue at the end of a Conwy or Llugwy day.

accommodation.name: Plas y Brenin
accommodation.description: On-site accommodation at the National Outdoor Centre for course attendees and casual residents. Sensible base if you're doing a paddling course or a few river days from a central Snowdonia location.
accommodation.nearestSpot: Llynnau Mymbyr (on site); Conwy / Llugwy 10-15 minutes

accommodation.name: Llyn Gwynant Campsite
accommodation.description: Lakeside campsite with on-site SUP and kayak hire for guests, plus stunning mountain backdrop. Good base for combining paddling with hiking days on the Watkin Path.
accommodation.nearestSpot: Llyn Gwynant (on site); Watkin Path trailhead 5 minutes

accommodation.name: Bala Backpackers
accommodation.description: Budget bunkhouse in Bala town, walking distance to the Llyn Tegid foreshore and Bala Adventure & Watersports. Natural choice for a flat-water weekend.

accommodation.name: YHA Snowdon Llanberis
accommodation.description: Budget hostel in Llanberis, walking distance to Llyn Padarn and the Snowdonia Watersports base.
